summary: Explains why the IPv6 flow label specification in RFC 3697 needed to change. Published proposals for using the label conflicted with the original text, and the label saw little real use, partly because of unclear wording. It motivates the changes made in RFC 6437 and is informational.

eli5.summary: A sticker was meant to group related packets, but the rules for it were fuzzy so nobody used it much. This explains why to clarify the rules and give a bit more freedom.

questions: why was the ipv6 flow label updated
what is the ipv6 flow label

how should ipv6 flow labels be chosen
subtitle: Why the IPv6 flow label rules of RFC 3697 were too strict to be useful, and what should change.

tldr.problem: The IPv6 flow label is hardly used, partly because the wording of its specification in RFC 3697 is unclear and conflicts with many proposed uses.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains the problems and motivates a revision: any node may set the label, labels should be uniformly distributed, and strict immutability is dropped. The normative text is in RFC 6437.
tldr.outcome: Stateless load distribution becomes the expected default use, while the label stays an unprotected best-effort hint.

today: RFC 6436 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is rationale only; the normative flow label rules are in RFC 6437.

sections.title: The Flow Label Before the Update
sections.content:
The flow label field in the IPv6 header was left Experimental by RFC 2460. RFC 3697 then specified it with three rules: (a) the value set by the source MUST be delivered unchanged, (b) nodes MUST NOT assume any mathematical or other properties of the values, and (c) router performance SHOULD NOT depend on the distribution of values, since the label bits alone make poor material for a hash key.

RFC 3697 gave no default method for choosing a value, and the expected signaling methods were never standardized, apart from a pre-existing option in RSVP (RFC 2205). So most hosts simply set the label to zero. This document does not formally update RFC 3697. It is background for RFC 6437.
sections.eli5: The sticker had three strict rules and no instructions for what to write on it, so most people left it blank.

sections.title: How the Old Rules Held Things Back
sections.content:
Rule (a) rules out using the label as a dynamic routing tag, a choice made in early IPv6 design. It also forbids clearing the label for security reasons, and nothing can use the label unless hosts set it. The field is unprotected: IPv6 has no header checksum, and the label is not in transport pseudo-header checksums or IPsec checksums, so malicious changes cannot be detected. It could also carry covert data. The word "immutable" is confusing because the field does not actually have that property.

Rules (b) and (c) were often over-read. A router that knows by configuration or signaling how labels were assigned may use that knowledge, and the word "alone" in rule (c) means a router may combine the label with other data in a hash for load distribution.

RFC 6294 surveys proposals that need routers to change the label, or to encode meaning in its bits. These appear to infringe the rules. Others, based on a source choosing a pseudo-random label per flow, are compatible.
sections.eli5: The rules said nobody could change the sticker, but nobody could stop a prankster from changing it either. And people misread the rules as banning things that were allowed.

sections.title: The Two Options and the Chosen Direction
sections.content:
The RFC describes a dilemma between two options. Option 1 discourages locally defined or stateful use and strengthens RFC 3697 so that hosts should set a label, which encourages load distribution. Option 2 relaxes the rules to encourage local or stateful use, which makes the label completely mutable and excludes end-to-end uses.

After debate in 2010 and 2011 the view was that simplicity should prevail. Defining quality-of-service semantics or splitting the label into sub-fields would not be efficient or deployable in high-speed routers, and stateless load distribution is the best simple application. Because modifications cannot be detected, any use is a best-effort optimization, and a packet with a changed or zero label should never cause a hard failure.
sections.eli5: People could keep the sticker strict or make it free-for-all. They picked a simple middle: use it to spread traffic evenly, and never let a missing or changed sticker break anything.

sections.title: Changes to the Specification
sections.content:
The label defaults to zero, which is what an overwhelming proportion of IPv6 packets carry. The authors therefore expect no operational difficulty from a careful change. The proposed changes are:

  • Any node, not just the source, may set the label. A first-hop or ingress router may set it if the source has not.
  • Sources should set a uniformly distributed label, using a hash function or a pseudo-random number generator. Sequential assignment is definitely not recommended, to avoid guessability.
  • Stateless methods are recommended as the default. Stateful methods remain possible but must also send uniformly distributed values, because a border router cannot tell by inspection whether a value is uniformly distributed.
  • Once set, the value must not be changed, with qualifications since the field is unprotected. Labels exported to the Internet should be zero or uniformly distributed.

Appendix A lists rejected alternatives: a flow label domain, using the most significant bit of the label to mark local labels, and using a DSCP in the Traffic Class octet.
sections.eli5: New rules: anyone helping the packet along may fill in the sticker, pick a random-looking number, and then leave it alone.

sections.title: Practical Consequences
sections.content:
Hosts that are not updated keep sending zero labels. Conforming hosts choose uniformly distributed labels between 1 and 0xFFFFF, and an ingress router may do the same for hosts that send zero. The default expected use is stateless load distribution, such as the ECMP and link aggregation usage in RFC 6438. Hosts and routers that ignore the label are unaffected. In general, hosts are assumed to ignore the label on receipt.

The security section simply points to RFC 6437 and a work-in-progress security assessment of the flow label.
sections.eli5: Old devices carry on as before. New ones add a random-looking number that helps spread traffic over several paths.
